Waiting should not become an excuse for inactivity.

Continue to work, learn, serve, prepare, and fulfil your responsibilities.

3. Develop courage during uncertain seasons.

Psalm 27:14 connects waiting with courage and inner strength.

This is important because waiting can test your emotional stability. You may experience disappointment when other people appear to be progressing faster than you. You may feel embarrassed when people ask questions about your situation.

Do not allow these pressures to make you abandon sound judgment or biblical convictions.

Courage is not the absence of concern. It is the willingness to remain faithful and take responsible action despite uncertainty.

4. Resist the temptation to force outcomes through compromise.

Impatience can make people accept dishonest shortcuts.

Someone desperate for money may enter fraudulent activities. Someone desperate for a relationship may tolerate manipulation or abuse. Someone desperate for success may sacrifice integrity to gain recognition.

The fact that an opportunity is available does not mean it is right.

Do not sacrifice your values to obtain something you believe you cannot wait for.

5. Use the waiting season for preparation.

Waiting can become a valuable season of development.

If you are waiting for a professional opportunity, improve your skills. If you are praying for greater responsibility, develop your capacity to serve. If you desire financial stability, learn budgeting and responsible money management.

Preparation does not guarantee a particular outcome, but it can help you respond wisely when opportunities arise.

6. Remember that God's presence is more important than the speed of your progress.

A person can achieve a desired goal and still live without peace, integrity, or spiritual direction.

Your relationship with God should not be reduced to receiving immediate answers to requests.

Learn to seek God for who He is, not only for what you hope He will provide.

The waiting season can deepen your faith, develop patience, and teach you to depend on God's strength.

Practical Illustration

A graduate applies for several jobs but receives repeated rejections. At first, he becomes discouraged and begins to believe that his education has been wasted.

After seeking counsel, he realises that his interview skills need improvement and that he lacks certain practical competencies required in his field.

He begins taking relevant courses, improves his CV, volunteers to gain experience, and continues applying for suitable opportunities.

He does not know exactly when the desired job will come, but he refuses to allow waiting to become a season of wasted potential.
devotionals.reflection:
1. What am I currently waiting for?
2. Has impatience tempted me to make decisions that conflict with my values?
3. Am I neglecting present responsibilities because I am focused on future expectations?
4. What can I learn, improve, or prepare while I wait?
5. Is my confidence in God dependent only on receiving the answer I desire?
devotionals.lesson: Waiting on God does not mean abandoning responsibility; it means trusting Him while remaining faithful, prepared, and courageous.
devotionals.prayer: Heavenly Father, strengthen my heart in every season of waiting. Deliver me from impatience, discouragement, fear, and destructive comparison. Give me wisdom to recognise what I should be doing now, courage to remain faithful, and patience to trust Your direction. Keep me from compromising my convictions in an attempt to force an outcome. Let my waiting season become a season of growth, preparation, and deeper dependence on You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Identify one important matter you have been waiting on. Write down what is within your control and what is beyond your control. Commit to one practical preparation step today, and deliberately surrender the outcome to God in prayer.

devotionals.title: Live One Day at a Time
devotionals.keyVerse: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
devotionals.introduction:
Life is lived one day at a time, but many people spend much of their present worrying about tomorrow or regretting yesterday.

Some are constantly anxious about what may happen next week, next month, or next year. Others remain emotionally trapped by decisions they made several years ago. As a result, they struggle to give proper attention to the opportunities, responsibilities, and relationships available to them today.

Jesus addressed this human tendency in Matthew 6:34. He taught His followers not to be consumed by anxiety about tomorrow because each day has its own concerns.

The instruction does not mean that Christians should refuse to plan for the future. Scripture encourages diligence, wisdom, and preparation. Proverbs 21:5, for example, commends the plans of the diligent.

Rather, Jesus warns against allowing tomorrow's uncertainties to dominate today's life.

A meaningful life requires the wisdom to prepare for the future while remaining fully responsible for the present.

1. Stop allowing tomorrow's uncertainties to steal today's peace.

You may not know what next month will bring. You may be uncertain about your finances, employment, health, family, or other important matters.

Worrying excessively does not give you control over the future.

It can, however, drain your energy, affect your concentration, and prevent you from dealing effectively with the matters before you.

Whenever you become overwhelmed by tomorrow, ask yourself: “What is the most responsible thing I can do today?”

Focus on that step.

2. Give today's responsibilities your best attention.

Your present life is made up of ordinary responsibilities that deserve attention.

If you are a student, study diligently today. If you are a parent, give your children meaningful attention today. If you are employed, fulfil your responsibilities honestly today. If you are building a business, serve your customers well today.

Do not become so preoccupied with a future achievement that you neglect the work required to move toward it.

3. Plan ahead without living in fear.

Planning is wise; uncontrolled anxiety is not.

You can prepare a budget, develop a career plan, schedule medical appointments, organise your family responsibilities, and establish realistic goals.

The difference is that planning identifies actions, while worry repeatedly imagines problems without necessarily producing solutions.

Make the preparations you reasonably can, then refuse to spend all your emotional energy trying to control what you cannot predict.

4. Learn to appreciate the opportunities within each day.

Every day provides opportunities that may never return in exactly the same form.

You can encourage someone, learn something useful, apologise, strengthen a relationship, complete a responsibility, or take a step toward a worthwhile goal.

Some people postpone meaningful living until they become wealthy, famous, married, employed, or financially comfortable.

But life is happening now.

Do not wait for perfect conditions before expressing love, practising gratitude, serving others, and developing yourself.

5. Correct today's mistakes instead of carrying them unnecessarily.

If you have made a mistake, acknowledge it and take appropriate steps to correct it.

If you have offended someone, apologise where appropriate. If you have neglected an important responsibility, make a plan to address it.

Do not spend every day condemning yourself for yesterday while repeating the same behaviour today.

Learn from the past, take responsibility in the present, and prepare wisely for the future.

6. Remember that every day is an opportunity to honour God.

Colossians 3:17 teaches that whatever we do in word or deed should be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God.

Your ordinary activities can become expressions of faithfulness.

You do not need to stand on a public platform to live meaningfully. You can honour God through honest work, responsible decisions, kindness, prayer, service, and love within your immediate environment.

A meaningful year is built through meaningful days.

Practical Illustration

A father becomes increasingly anxious about the future of his family. He worries about school fees, household expenses, his children's education, and his retirement.

His anxiety begins to affect his sleep and his relationship with his family.

After reflecting on Jesus' teaching, he decides to take practical steps. He reviews the family budget, discusses financial priorities with his spouse, identifies unnecessary expenses, and begins a realistic savings plan.

He also makes a deliberate effort to spend quality time with his children instead of allowing financial worries to consume every evening.

He has not solved every future challenge, but he has stopped allowing tomorrow's uncertainty to destroy today's responsibilities and relationships.
devotionals.reflection:
1. Am I spending too much time worrying about what may happen tomorrow?
2. Which present responsibilities have I neglected because of future concerns?
3. Do I understand the difference between wise planning and destructive anxiety?
4. What meaningful opportunity is available to me today?
5. How can I honour God more intentionally through my activities today?
devotionals.lesson: Prepare wisely for tomorrow, learn from yesterday, but give today's responsibilities your full and faithful attention.
devotionals.prayer: Father, teach me to live wisely and faithfully each day. Deliver me from excessive worry about tomorrow and unnecessary regret about yesterday. Give me wisdom to plan responsibly, courage to face today's challenges, and grace to recognise the opportunities You have placed before me. Help me to use my time meaningfully, fulfil my responsibilities faithfully, and honour You in my everyday activities. In Jesus' name, Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Write down the three most important responsibilities you need to address today. Give each one deliberate attention before allowing unnecessary distractions to take over. Also, identify one person you can encourage or appreciate today. Practise living intentionally rather than allowing worry to consume your day.

devotionals.title: Examine Your Life and Realign Your Direction
devotionals.keyVerse: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
devotionals.introduction:
The end of a month is more than a calendar transition. It is an opportunity to pause, reflect, evaluate, and make necessary adjustments.

Many people are quick to evaluate other people's lives but rarely take time to examine their own. They can identify the weaknesses of colleagues, friends, family members, leaders, and even the church, yet remain unaware of areas in their own lives that require correction.

Paul's instruction in 2 Corinthians 13:5 challenges believers to examine themselves. In its immediate context, he was addressing the Corinthians' spiritual condition and their need to consider whether their lives genuinely reflected the faith they professed.

This instruction remains important for every believer. We must not assume that because we started well, everything is automatically going well.

A meaningful life requires regular self-examination.

As January comes to an end, this is an appropriate moment to examine your direction, evaluate your progress, and realign your life with God's purposes.

1. Examine the condition of your spiritual life.

Your relationship with God deserves regular attention.

Ask yourself whether your prayer life is growing, whether you are developing a deeper understanding of Scripture, and whether your conduct reflects the character of Christ.

Do not measure spiritual growth only by the number of church services you attend, positions you occupy, or religious activities you perform.

Consider the fruit of your life.

Are you growing in love, patience, humility, self-control, forgiveness, faithfulness, and obedience?

Galatians 5:22–23 identifies the fruit of the Spirit as qualities that should increasingly be evident in the life of a believer.

2. Examine the direction of your personal development.

Are you becoming more disciplined, knowledgeable, responsible, and emotionally mature?

Have you identified areas where you need additional training or improvement?

A person who refuses to evaluate personal development may continue repeating the same habits while expecting different outcomes.

Be honest about your strengths and weaknesses. Celebrate genuine progress without becoming proud, and acknowledge areas of weakness without surrendering to discouragement.

3. Examine the quality of your relationships.

How are you treating the people around you?

Are you a source of encouragement or unnecessary conflict? Do you listen when others speak? Are you dependable? Do you respect boundaries? Are you willing to apologise when you are wrong?

Consider your relationships with family members, friends, colleagues, neighbours, and fellow believers.

Where reconciliation is possible and appropriate, take responsible steps toward peace. Where boundaries are necessary for safety and well-being, establish them wisely.

4. Examine how you are using your time and resources.

Time, money, abilities, and opportunities are important resources.

Have you used them responsibly during the month? Have you allowed unnecessary distractions to consume time that should have been devoted to important responsibilities?

Have you been financially disciplined? Have you invested in your growth? Have you used your abilities to contribute positively to the lives of others?

Honest evaluation helps you recognise where improvement is necessary.

5. Identify what must change.

Self-examination is incomplete if it ends with discovering weaknesses but produces no corrective action.

If you identify indiscipline, develop a practical routine. If you identify poor financial management, establish a budget. If you identify neglect of prayer, create a realistic prayer schedule. If you identify unhealthy communication, practise listening and responsible speech.

Do not attempt to change everything through emotional excitement. Identify priorities and develop measurable steps.

6. Realign your goals with God's principles.

Not every goal that appears attractive is necessarily worth pursuing.

Some ambitions may be driven by competition, pride, insecurity, or the desire to impress others.

As you review your goals, ask whether they are consistent with biblical values, responsible stewardship, love for God, and service to people.

A successful year is not simply one in which you accumulate achievements. It is one in which your progress is consistent with a life of faithfulness and godly purpose.

7. Enter the next month with renewed commitment.

February begins tomorrow, and its central theme will address the serious subject of suicide.

As you conclude January, carry forward the lessons of purposeful living. Remember that the value of life is not determined by wealth, achievement, social status, or the absence of challenges.

Every human life has dignity and should be treated with compassion. When people experience deep emotional pain, they need understanding, support, and appropriate help.

Let the understanding of life's value influence how you treat yourself and others.

Practical Illustration

A school administrator reviews the activities of the first month of the year. Rather than simply celebrating the number of meetings held, he examines the actual results.

He discovers that staff communication has improved, but record-keeping remains poor. Some administrative responsibilities are not clearly assigned, and certain parents have not received timely information.

Instead of blaming everyone, he identifies the gaps, assigns responsibilities, establishes reporting procedures, and sets measurable targets for February.

The review does not erase the shortcomings of January, but it helps the organisation enter February with better direction.

Your personal life deserves the same level of honest evaluation.
devotionals.reflection:
1. What have I learned about myself during January?
2. Has my relationship with God received the attention it deserves?
3. Which habits have helped me grow, and which habits have hindered my progress?
4. Have I treated the people around me with love, respect, and responsibility?
5. What must I stop, start, or improve as I enter February?
6. Are my goals consistent with God's principles and the kind of person I desire to become?
devotionals.lesson: A meaningful life requires regular self-examination, honest evaluation, and the willingness to make necessary changes.
devotionals.prayer: Heavenly Father, thank You for bringing me to the end of January. Search my heart and reveal every area that requires correction, healing, growth, and realignment. Forgive my shortcomings and give me the humility to learn from my experiences. Strengthen my spiritual life, improve my character, guide my decisions, and help me manage my time and resources faithfully. As I enter a new month, let me walk with greater wisdom, compassion, discipline, and commitment to Your purposes. In Jesus' name, Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint:
Conduct a personal review of January under these six areas:

1. Spiritual life: What has improved in my relationship with God?
2. Character: Which attitude or habit needs correction?
3. Relationships: Who needs my attention, encouragement, forgiveness, or an apology?
4. Work and responsibilities: What have I done well, and what needs improvement?
5. Finances and resources: Have I managed what I have responsibly?
6. Personal development: What knowledge, skill, or discipline should I develop next?

Write down three lessons from January, three things you need to change, and three practical goals for February.

Do not enter a new month merely because the calendar has changed. Enter it with a clearer heart, better understanding, and a stronger commitment to live meaningfully.

devotionals.title: Your Life Is Not a Mistake: You Were Created for a Purpose
devotionals.keyVerse: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Genesis 1:26–27; Psalm 139:13–16; Ephesians 2:10.

One of the greatest battles a human being can face is the struggle to find meaning in life. When life becomes unbearable, expectations are disappointed, relationships collapse, financial difficulties become overwhelming or personal failures seem impossible to overcome, some people begin to question the value of their existence.

They may begin to think that nobody needs them, their existence is a burden, nothing good can happen again or the world would be better without them.

These thoughts can become dangerous when someone begins to believe that death is the only escape from emotional pain.

However, God's Word presents a different perspective: YOUR LIFE IS NOT AN ACCIDENT, AND YOUR EXISTENCE IS NOT WITHOUT MEANING.

Jeremiah 1:5 reveals that before Jeremiah was born, God already knew him and had a purpose for his life. This teaches us that human value does not begin with achievements, wealth, educational qualifications, marriage or public recognition. Your value begins with God.

1. GOD KNEW YOU BEFORE PEOPLE KNEW YOU.

People may misunderstand, reject or abandon you. Their inability to appreciate you does not cancel God's knowledge of you. You are not defined by people's opinions.

2. YOUR MISTAKES DO NOT CANCEL YOUR EXISTENCE.

Some people contemplate suicide because of mistakes they have made. They may have lost money, failed examinations, experienced business collapse or damaged important relationships. But making a mistake does not mean you have become a mistake. Peter denied Jesus three times, yet Jesus restored him (John 21:15–17).

3. YOUR PRESENT CONDITION DOES NOT DEFINE YOUR ENTIRE FUTURE.

Joseph experienced betrayal, slavery and imprisonment before becoming a national leader (Genesis 37–41). His painful experiences did not make his life meaningless. A difficult chapter is not the entire story.

4. HUMAN LIFE CARRIES DIVINE VALUE.

Genesis 1:27 teaches that humanity was created in God's image. Every human being deserves dignity, protection, compassion and care. Nobody should be made to feel that their life is disposable because of poverty, disability, unemployment, rejection or personal failure.

5. YOU DESERVE HELP WHEN LIFE BECOMES OVERWHELMING.

Faith does not require you to pretend that you are emotionally strong when you are struggling. You can pray and also seek help from a psychologist, psychiatrist, counsellor or medical professional. Seeking help is not spiritual failure.
devotionals.reflection:
Have you measured your worth by what you have achieved, what people think about you or what you have lost? Have you allowed a temporary situation to make you question the value of your entire existence?

Remember: You are more than your mistakes, disappointments and present circumstances. A difficult season does not cancel your worth.
devotionals.lesson: Never allow a temporary situation, personal failure or another person's rejection to determine the value of your life.
devotionals.prayer: Father, thank You for the gift of life. Deliver me from every thought, experience and circumstance that makes me question the value of my existence. Restore my sense of purpose, renew my hope and help me recognise the preciousness of the life You have given me, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Write down five reasons your life is worth living. Identify one person who genuinely cares about you and reach out to that person today. If you are experiencing suicidal thoughts, tell someone you trust and seek professional support rather than facing those thoughts alone.

devotionals.title: When Life Becomes Too Heavy: God Understands Your Pain
devotionals.keyVerse: But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree: and he requested for himself that he might die; and said, It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Psalm 34:18; Matthew 11:28–30; Psalm 42:5–11; Isaiah 41:10.

One of the most remarkable biblical accounts of emotional distress is the experience of Prophet Elijah.

Elijah was a mighty prophet. He confronted false prophets, demonstrated the power of God on Mount Carmel and witnessed extraordinary divine intervention. Yet this same man reached a point where he requested that God should take his life.

After confronting the prophets of Baal, Jezebel threatened to kill him. Elijah became frightened, fled into the wilderness, became exhausted and expressed a desire to die.

This teaches us an important truth: BEING SPIRITUALLY GIFTED DOES NOT MAKE A PERSON IMMUNE TO EMOTIONAL SUFFERING.

A person can be prayerful and still experience depression. Someone can preach powerfully and still struggle privately. Someone can encourage thousands and still need encouragement.

1. EMOTIONAL EXHAUSTION IS REAL.

Elijah had experienced intense confrontation, pressure and danger. His physical and emotional resources were depleted. Sometimes, what people interpret as spiritual weakness may involve severe stress, exhaustion, grief, trauma or a mental health condition.

2. THREATS AND FEAR CAN OVERWHELM THE HUMAN MIND.

Elijah's emotional condition deteriorated after Jezebel threatened his life. People can experience overwhelming distress following threats, bullying, domestic abuse, public humiliation, financial crises and traumatic experiences.

3. GOD DID NOT CONDEMN ELIJAH FOR EXPRESSING HIS DISTRESS.

In 1 Kings 19:5–8, God provided food, water and rest for Elijah. Before Elijah received further instructions, he received care. Sometimes, people do not first need a sermon. They need someone to listen, help them rest and connect them with appropriate care.

4. GOD ADDRESSED ELIJAH'S CONDITION WITH COMPASSION AND DIRECTION.

In 1 Kings 19:9–18, God engaged Elijah and gave him direction. Elijah's story did not end under the juniper tree. His season of despair was not the conclusion of his assignment.

5. NEVER CONFUSE A PAINFUL SEASON WITH A PERMANENT CONDITION.

Emotional pain can make the future appear hopeless. However, feelings are not always accurate predictions of what will happen. Depression and suicidal thoughts are treatable, and people can recover with appropriate support.

If you are overwhelmed, speak to someone trustworthy and seek professional assessment. If you feel you may act on suicidal thoughts, do not remain alone. Go to the nearest hospital emergency department.
devotionals.reflection:
Are you carrying an emotional burden that nobody knows about? Have you become so accustomed to encouraging others that you have forgotten that you also need encouragement?

God sees the pain behind your smile. You do not have to pretend that everything is fine.
devotionals.lesson: Never condemn yourself or another person for experiencing emotional distress. Recognise the pain, seek appropriate help and allow compassionate support to become part of the healing process.
devotionals.prayer: Father, in every season when life becomes overwhelming, uphold me by Your strength. Heal my wounded heart, renew my mind and surround me with people who genuinely care. Give me the courage to speak about my struggles and the wisdom to receive the help I need, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Check on someone who has been unusually withdrawn, discouraged or emotionally overwhelmed. Listen without judging. If you are the person struggling, take one step towards receiving support today.

devotionals.title: When the Mind Says There Is No Hope: Challenge the Lie of Hopelessness
devotionals.keyVerse:
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.

It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.

They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Romans 8:38–39; Psalm 30:5; Isaiah 43:18–19; 2 Corinthians 4:8–9.

Hopelessness is one of the most dangerous experiences associated with suicidal thinking.

It is the feeling that nothing can improve, nobody can help, tomorrow will be worse and there is no meaningful reason to continue living.

When hopelessness becomes deeply rooted, a person may stop seeing possibilities even when help is available.

We must understand the difference between what we are experiencing and what we conclude about our future.

PAIN IS AN EXPERIENCE; HOPELESSNESS IS THE CONCLUSION THAT PAIN HAS PERMANENTLY DESTROYED EVERY POSSIBILITY OF A BETTER FUTURE.

That conclusion can be challenged.

The writer of Lamentations was not writing from a comfortable environment. The book reflects the grief, destruction and suffering associated with Jerusalem's devastation. Yet in the middle of sorrow, the writer declares: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope."

1. YOUR MIND NEEDS THE RIGHT INFORMATION DURING DIFFICULT SEASONS.

When a person is overwhelmed, negative thoughts may become repetitive: "I am useless." "Nothing will ever work." "Nobody cares." "I cannot survive this."

These thoughts should not automatically be accepted as facts. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts needs compassionate support and, where appropriate, professional help to challenge harmful thinking patterns.

2. HOPE DOES NOT MEAN DENYING REALITY.

Christian hope is not pretending that problems do not exist. It is recognising that problems exist without accepting that they have the final authority over our lives.

A person can acknowledge financial difficulties and still seek solutions. A person can acknowledge marital disappointment and still receive counselling. A person can acknowledge failure and still begin again.

3. GOD'S MERCY PROVIDES ROOM FOR ANOTHER BEGINNING.

Lamentations 3:22–23 teaches that God's mercies are new every morning. Yesterday's disappointment does not have to determine today's possibilities. Every new day creates opportunities for support, recovery, reconciliation, learning and change.

4. DO NOT MAKE PERMANENT DECISIONS FROM TEMPORARY EMOTIONAL CONDITIONS.

Severe emotional pain can narrow a person's ability to see alternatives. Suicidal thoughts must be treated seriously and urgently.

When such thoughts arise, postpone any action, move away from anything you could use to harm yourself, stay with a trusted person and seek immediate professional assistance. You do not need to solve your entire life today. You need to remain safe and receive help through this moment.

5. HOPE CAN BE REBUILT THROUGH SMALL, PRACTICAL STEPS.

Sometimes, the first step towards recovery is not a dramatic breakthrough. It may be speaking honestly with someone, visiting a mental health professional, receiving help with an overwhelming problem, reconnecting with a supportive family member or establishing a healthy routine.

Small steps can become part of a meaningful recovery journey.
devotionals.reflection:
What thoughts have been controlling your interpretation of life? Have you concluded that because something has gone wrong, everything has gone wrong?

Are you allowing yesterday's disappointment to determine your expectations for tomorrow?

Hopelessness is not a prophecy. Your present pain does not have the authority to declare that your future is finished.
devotionals.lesson: Never treat your darkest thoughts as the final truth about your life. Challenge hopeless conclusions, seek support and take one safe step towards recovery at a time.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, renew my mind and restore my hope. Deliver me from destructive thoughts, overwhelming discouragement and every belief that makes me feel that life has no meaning. Help me recognise the possibilities ahead and give me the courage to take the necessary steps towards healing, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint:
Write down three painful thoughts that have discouraged you recently. Beside each one, write a more balanced and hopeful response.

For example:
"I have failed" becomes "I experienced a failure, but I can learn and seek another opportunity."

"Nobody cares" becomes "I need to reach out and allow someone to support me."

"My future is finished" becomes "I cannot predict my entire future from today's circumstances."

devotionals.title: Recognising the Silent Cry: Never Ignore the Warning Signs
devotionals.keyVerse: If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Galatians 6:2; Romans 12:15; Proverbs 31:8–9; James 1:19.

One of the greatest mistakes society makes concerning suicide is assuming that people who are struggling will always announce their intentions clearly.

Many people suffer silently. Some withdraw from family and friends. Some stop participating in activities they previously enjoyed. Some express feelings of worthlessness, hopelessness or being a burden. Others make preparations to end their lives.

Suicide prevention is not only the responsibility of psychologists, psychiatrists and medical professionals. Families, churches, schools, workplaces and communities also have important roles to play.

The Church must become a place where struggling people can speak without fear of condemnation.

1. LEARN TO RECOGNISE CHANGES IN BEHAVIOUR.

Potential warning signs include:

- Persistent expressions of hopelessness.
- Talking about wanting to die or kill oneself.
- Feelings of worthlessness or being a burden.
- Increasing isolation and withdrawal.
- Giving away valued possessions unexpectedly.
- Saying goodbye in an unusual or final manner.
- Searching for ways to end one's life.
- Sudden changes in mood, behaviour or sleeping patterns.
- Increased alcohol or substance misuse.
- Severe agitation, emotional distress or reckless behaviour.

These signs do not automatically mean someone will attempt suicide. However, they should never be ignored, especially when several occur together or there is a noticeable change in behaviour.

2. TAKE SUICIDAL STATEMENTS SERIOUSLY.

If somebody says, "I am tired of living," do not immediately dismiss the statement as attention-seeking.

Ask calmly and directly: "Are you thinking about suicide or hurting yourself?"

Asking directly about suicide does not put the idea into someone's mind. It can create an opportunity for honest communication and appropriate intervention.

3. LISTEN WITHOUT CONDEMNATION.

Avoid statements such as:
"You are not a serious Christian."
"You don't have enough faith."
"Other people have worse problems."
"Stop thinking nonsense."
"You are only looking for attention."

Such statements can increase shame and isolation.

Instead, say:
"I am glad you told me."
"I care about you."
"You do not have to face this alone."
"Let us get the help you need."

4. DO NOT LEAVE A PERSON IN IMMEDIATE DANGER ALONE.

If someone may act on suicidal thoughts:

- Stay with the person or arrange for a trusted adult to remain with them.
- Ask whether they have a plan, access to anything they could use, or an intention to act soon.
- Help them move away from medicines, weapons or other dangerous items, provided it is safe to do so.
- Contact emergency services or take them to the nearest hospital emergency department.
- Do not promise to keep an immediate suicide risk secret.

A person at immediate risk needs urgent professional assessment, not merely prayer or a promise to be strong.

5. THE CHURCH MUST BECOME PART OF THE SUPPORT SYSTEM.

Church leaders and chaplains should be trained to recognise warning signs, listen compassionately, maintain appropriate confidentiality and refer people to qualified mental health professionals.

Spiritual care and professional mental healthcare can work together.

6. SUPPORT SHOULD CONTINUE AFTER THE IMMEDIATE CRISIS.

Do not disappear after somebody has experienced a suicidal crisis. Continue checking on the person, encourage professional follow-up and help them rebuild meaningful social connections.
devotionals.reflection:
How observant are you towards the emotional condition of people around you? Do you notice when somebody becomes unusually quiet, withdrawn or hopeless?

Are you creating an environment where people can discuss their struggles without being judged?

Sometimes, the person who needs help is sitting beside you in church, working with you in the office or living in your house.
devotionals.lesson: Never ignore expressions of hopelessness or suicidal thoughts. Compassionate listening, timely intervention and professional support can help save lives.
devotionals.prayer: Father, make me sensitive to the silent cries of people around me. Give me wisdom to recognise distress, compassion to listen without condemnation and courage to take appropriate action when someone's life is in danger. Use me as an instrument of hope, protection and restoration, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Reach out to someone who may be struggling emotionally. Ask how they are genuinely doing. Listen patiently. If they disclose suicidal thoughts, take them seriously and help them access appropriate professional support.

devotionals.title: Asking for Help Is Not Weakness: The Courage to Seek Help
devotionals.keyVerse: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Ecclesiastes 4:9–10; Proverbs 11:14; James 5:16; Mark 2:3–5.

One of the greatest obstacles preventing people from receiving help is the belief that asking for help is a sign of weakness.

Some people believe they must solve every problem independently. Others are afraid of being judged, embarrassed or misunderstood.

Some Christians believe that consulting a mental health professional means they lack faith in God.

These beliefs can become dangerous when someone is experiencing suicidal thoughts.

We must establish an important truth: GOD NEVER DESIGNED HUMAN BEINGS TO CARRY EVERY BURDEN ALONE.

Galatians 6:2 commands believers to bear one another's burdens. Christianity is not merely about personal spirituality; it also involves compassion, mutual responsibility and practical care.

1. ASKING FOR HELP IS AN ACT OF COURAGE.
It takes courage to admit that you are struggling. It takes courage to tell somebody that you are not coping. It takes courage to visit a counsellor, psychologist, psychiatrist or doctor.

You are not less valuable because you need assistance.

2. GOD USES PEOPLE AS INSTRUMENTS OF HELP.
In Mark 2:3–5, four men carried a paralysed man to Jesus because he could not reach Him by himself.

Their action demonstrates the importance of supportive relationships.

Sometimes, a struggling person needs somebody to help them take the next step. That help may come through a family member, pastor, trained counsellor, doctor, friend or community support organisation.

3. PROFESSIONAL MENTAL HEALTHCARE IS NOT OPPOSED TO FAITH.
Mental health conditions are real health concerns. Depression, bipolar disorder, trauma-related conditions and other mental health challenges can require professional assessment and treatment.

A person may need counselling, psychotherapy, medication, medical monitoring or a combination of appropriate interventions.

Prayer can provide spiritual comfort, strength and encouragement, but it should never be used as a substitute for necessary medical care.

We must stop telling people to abandon treatment because they should simply pray harder.

4. CHOOSE THE RIGHT PEOPLE TO CONFIDE IN.
Not everybody has the emotional maturity or professional competence to handle sensitive disclosures.

Choose people who are compassionate, trustworthy, willing to listen without condemnation, responsible and able to help you access professional support.

If the first person you approach does not respond appropriately, do not conclude that nobody can help you. Approach another trusted person or qualified professional.

5. BUILD RELATIONSHIPS BEFORE CRISES OCCUR.
Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 teaches that two are better than one because when one falls, the other can help.

Healthy relationships provide emotional support and reduce isolation.

Families should develop cultures of communication. Churches should provide accessible counselling and referral systems. Schools should create safe environments where students can discuss emotional challenges. Workplaces should take employee mental wellbeing seriously.

6. IF YOU ARE STRUGGLING, TAKE IMMEDIATE STEPS TOWARDS SAFETY.
If you are thinking about suicide:

- Tell someone you trust clearly what you are experiencing.
- Do not remain alone if you feel you may act on those thoughts.
- Move away from medicines, weapons or other items you could use to harm yourself.
- Seek urgent medical or mental health assistance.
- If you are in immediate danger, go to the nearest hospital emergency department or contact local emergency services.

You do not have to wait until your situation becomes unbearable before asking for help.
devotionals.reflection:
Have you been suffering silently because you are afraid of what people will say? Have you allowed pride, shame or religious misconceptions to prevent you from receiving help?

Do you have people around you who can support you during difficult seasons?

Asking for help does not reduce your dignity. Sometimes, the bravest decision you can make is to tell somebody, "I am not okay, and I need help."
devotionals.lesson: You were not created to carry every burden alone. Seeking appropriate help is a responsible expression of wisdom, courage and respect for the gift of life.
devotionals.prayer: Father, deliver me from pride, shame and every misconception that prevents me from receiving necessary help. Surround me with compassionate and responsible people. Give me the courage to speak when I am struggling and make me an instrument of support to others. Let my life become a testimony of Your sustaining grace, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Identify three people you can confidently approach during difficult seasons. They may include a trusted family member, spiritual leader and qualified mental health professional. If you are currently struggling, contact one of them today and communicate honestly about your condition.

devotionals.title: Depression Is Not a Death Sentence: Understanding the Darkness Within
devotionals.keyVerse: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Psalm 34:18; 1 Kings 19:4–8; Isaiah 40:29–31; Romans 12:2.

Depression is one of the major mental health conditions that can increase a person's vulnerability to suicidal thoughts. It is more than occasional sadness, disappointment or having a bad day. Depression can affect how a person thinks, feels, sleeps, eats, relates with others and responds to everyday responsibilities.

A depressed person may smile publicly while experiencing deep emotional pain privately. Some continue working, attending church, raising children and fulfilling responsibilities while silently battling overwhelming sadness.

One dangerous mistake society makes is assuming that depression is simply a lack of faith, laziness or an unwillingness to be happy.

Depression is a genuine health condition that deserves understanding, proper assessment and treatment.

1. DEPRESSION IS MORE THAN ORDINARY SADNESS.
Ordinary sadness often follows a particular disappointment and may gradually improve. Depression can persist and interfere significantly with daily functioning.

Possible symptoms include persistent sadness, loss of interest, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep and appetite, and thoughts of death or suicide.

Only a qualified health professional can properly assess and diagnose depression.

2. DEPRESSION CAN AFFECT ANYBODY.
It does not respect age, gender, educational qualification, financial status, occupation or religious position.

A pastor can experience depression. A successful businessperson can experience depression. A student, married person, single parent or wealthy individual can also experience it.

Nobody should be ashamed of seeking help.

3. DEPRESSION CAN DISTORT THE WAY A PERSON SEES LIFE.
Depression can make someone believe that they are worthless, that their situation will never improve or that nobody cares about them.

These feelings can become overwhelming, but they are not reliable predictions of the future.

A person experiencing depression needs compassion, professional assessment and appropriate support.

4. DEPRESSION IS TREATABLE.
Depending on the individual's condition, treatment may include psychotherapy, medication, lifestyle adjustments, social support or a combination of interventions.

Prayer and spiritual encouragement can provide important support, but they should complement rather than replace necessary healthcare.

5. NEVER IGNORE SUICIDAL THOUGHTS ASSOCIATED WITH DEPRESSION.
When a depressed person begins expressing a desire to die, hopelessness or thoughts of suicide, take the situation seriously.

Listen without condemnation, stay with the person if there is immediate danger, reduce access to dangerous items where safe and obtain urgent professional assistance.
devotionals.reflection:
Have you ever dismissed somebody's depression as laziness or lack of faith?

Have you been hiding emotional pain because you are afraid of being judged?

Remember that depression is not a moral failure, and receiving treatment is not a spiritual defeat.
devotionals.lesson: Treat depression as a serious health condition requiring compassion, understanding and appropriate professional attention.
devotionals.prayer: Father, strengthen everyone experiencing depression and emotional darkness. Let Your comfort reach those who feel abandoned and hopeless. Give them access to compassionate people, qualified professionals and effective treatment. Restore hope, strengthen families and preserve lives, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Learn to recognise the signs of depression. Reach out to someone who may be struggling, and never discourage anyone from seeking professional mental healthcare.

devotionals.title: When Nobody Seems to Care: Overcoming Loneliness and Rejection
devotionals.keyVerse: When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Hebrews 13:5; Isaiah 49:15–16; Psalm 68:5–6; John 14:18.

One of the painful experiences that can affect human emotional wellbeing is loneliness.

Loneliness is not necessarily the absence of people. A person can live in a crowded house, attend a busy church, work in a large organisation and still feel completely alone.

Some people experience loneliness because of rejection, abandonment, divorce, bereavement, broken friendships, family conflicts or the inability to find meaningful relationships.

Others feel lonely because nobody seems interested in understanding what they are going through.

When loneliness becomes severe, it can contribute to hopelessness, depression and suicidal thinking.

However, God's Word reminds us that human rejection does not cancel divine love.

1. REJECTION DOES NOT MEAN YOU ARE UNWORTHY OF LOVE.
Some people have been rejected by parents, spouses, friends, employers or religious communities.

They may begin to conclude that something is fundamentally wrong with them.

But another person's inability or unwillingness to love you does not determine your worth.

Psalm 27:10 reminds us that even when earthly relationships fail, God remains faithful.

2. LONELINESS CAN AFFECT PEOPLE WHO APPEAR SUCCESSFUL.
Do not assume that someone is emotionally fulfilled because they are wealthy, educated, popular or surrounded by people.

Some people have thousands of social media followers but nobody they can confidently call when they are emotionally distressed.

Meaningful relationships are more important than the number of people around us.

3. LEARN TO COMMUNICATE YOUR EMOTIONAL NEEDS.
Some people withdraw because they believe nobody will understand them.

Although it may be difficult, take the courage to communicate with trustworthy people.

You can say, "I have been feeling lonely lately, and I would appreciate someone to talk to."

You do not have to explain everything perfectly before asking for companionship.

4. BUILD HEALTHY RELATIONSHIPS.
Join supportive communities, participate in meaningful activities and develop relationships with people who respect your dignity.

Churches should create welcoming environments where people are genuinely known, not merely counted as members.

5. DO NOT ALLOW REJECTION TO BECOME YOUR IDENTITY.
Jesus Himself experienced rejection, betrayal and abandonment, yet His life and mission were not defined by the rejection He experienced.

Your identity is greater than the people who walked away from you.

6. SEEK HELP WHEN LONELINESS BECOMES OVERWHELMING.
Persistent loneliness accompanied by depression or suicidal thoughts deserves professional attention.

Reach out to trusted people and qualified professionals. If you feel at risk of harming yourself, do not remain alone; seek emergency help.
devotionals.reflection:
Are you surrounded by people but emotionally disconnected?

Have you allowed rejection to make you believe that you are unlovable?

Are there people around you who need your friendship, attention and understanding?

Remember, being rejected by someone does not mean you have been rejected by life.
devotionals.lesson: Do not allow rejection to determine your identity. Develop healthy relationships and become a source of encouragement to others.
devotionals.prayer: Father, heal every wound of rejection, abandonment and loneliness. Connect me with healthy relationships and compassionate people. Deliver me from the belief that I am unwanted or unworthy of love. Make me an instrument of friendship, encouragement and restoration to those who feel forgotten, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Contact someone you have not spoken with for a while. Offer genuine friendship and encouragement. If you have been experiencing loneliness, take the initiative to connect with someone trustworthy today.

devotionals.title: When Financial Pressure Becomes Overwhelming: Your Life Is Worth More Than Money
devotionals.keyVerse: Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Matthew 6:31–34; Philippians 4:19; Psalm 37:25; 1 Timothy 6:6–10.

Financial difficulties are among the major pressures that can affect human emotional wellbeing.

Unemployment, business failure, accumulated debts, inability to provide for family members, unpaid salaries, failed investments and economic hardship can create enormous psychological pressure.

In societies where people are judged by their financial achievements, some individuals begin to measure their worth by the size of their bank accounts.

When financial expectations are not met, shame, anxiety, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts may develop.

We must understand this important truth: MONEY IS IMPORTANT, BUT HUMAN LIFE IS MORE IMPORTANT THAN MONEY.

1. FINANCIAL DIFFICULTIES DO NOT MAKE YOU A FAILURE AS A HUMAN BEING.
You may be poor today without being worthless.

You may have lost a business without losing your identity.

You may be indebted without losing your right to live.

Your financial condition is not the total definition of your existence.

2. DO NOT ALLOW FINANCIAL SHAME TO DESTROY YOUR LIFE.
Some people hide their financial difficulties because they are afraid of embarrassment.

They continue pretending that everything is fine while pressure increases.

Instead of suffering silently, speak with responsible people who can help you evaluate your situation and identify practical solutions.

3. FINANCIAL PROBLEMS REQUIRE PRACTICAL SOLUTIONS.
Depending on the situation, useful steps may include preparing a realistic budget, negotiating repayment arrangements, seeking financial counselling, exploring alternative employment, restructuring a business or asking trustworthy people for temporary assistance.

Avoid making desperate financial decisions that create additional problems.

4. GOD'S PROVISION DOES NOT ALWAYS COME THROUGH MIRACLES ALONE.
Sometimes provision comes through employment, new opportunities, education, responsible planning, business relationships, family assistance and community support.

Do not overlook practical opportunities while waiting for supernatural intervention.

5. NEVER EQUATE DEBT WITH THE END OF YOUR LIFE.
Debt can be stressful, but it can often be addressed through negotiation, structured repayment and appropriate financial advice.

If you are facing legal or financial pressure, seek competent advice instead of making decisions out of panic.

6. IF FINANCIAL PRESSURE IS PRODUCING SUICIDAL THOUGHTS, SEEK IMMEDIATE HELP.
Your life is worth more than your debts, business losses or financial reputation.

Tell someone you trust. Do not remain alone if you feel unsafe. Seek professional mental health assistance and urgent medical care if you may act on suicidal thoughts.
devotionals.reflection:
Have you allowed your financial condition to determine how you see yourself?

Are you suffering silently because you are ashamed of your financial situation?

Have you forgotten that you can rebuild financially without destroying yourself?

Your life is not a business transaction. Your value cannot be calculated in naira.
devotionals.lesson: Financial challenges should be confronted with wisdom, planning, patience and appropriate support, never with self-destruction.
devotionals.prayer: Father, strengthen everyone passing through financial hardship. Deliver them from destructive anxiety, shame and hopelessness. Open doors of legitimate opportunities, grant wisdom for financial decisions and connect them with responsible people who can provide practical assistance. Above all, preserve their lives and restore their hope, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Identify one financial challenge you have been avoiding. Take a practical step towards addressing it. If someone around you is experiencing financial distress, offer encouragement without humiliation or condemnation.

devotionals.title: When Relationships Break Down: You Can Survive Rejection and Heartbreak
devotionals.keyVerse: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Psalm 34:18; Isaiah 61:1–3; Romans 8:35–39; Proverbs 4:23.

Relationship problems can create some of the deepest emotional wounds people experience.

Broken marriages, failed engagements, unfaithfulness, separation, divorce, betrayal, rejection and the death of loved ones can leave people emotionally devastated.

For some individuals, the loss of a relationship becomes so painful that they begin to believe life is no longer worth living.

They may ask themselves:

"How can I live without this person?"
"Why did someone I loved so much abandon me?"
"Will anybody ever love me again?"
"How can I face the embarrassment of this separation?"

These questions reveal the emotional weight of heartbreak.

However, we must understand that THE END OF A RELATIONSHIP DOES NOT HAVE TO MEAN THE END OF YOUR LIFE.

1. RELATIONSHIP BREAKDOWN CAN CAUSE GENUINE EMOTIONAL PAIN.
We must never trivialise heartbreak.

A failed marriage or relationship can affect a person's identity, finances, family relationships, emotional stability and sense of security.

Allow people to grieve without mocking or dismissing their pain.

2. YOUR IDENTITY IS GREATER THAN YOUR RELATIONSHIP STATUS.
Being unmarried does not make you incomplete.

Being divorced does not make you worthless.

Being rejected does not mean you are unlovable.

Being betrayed does not mean you deserve suffering.

Your worth is not determined by whether someone chooses to remain in your life.

3. DO NOT MAKE PERMANENT DECISIONS DURING EMOTIONAL CRISES.
When heartbreak is intense, thinking can become clouded by anger, grief and desperation.

Avoid acting impulsively or making irreversible decisions while overwhelmed.

Seek emotional support and professional counselling where necessary.

If you are experiencing suicidal thoughts, tell someone immediately and obtain professional help.

4. FORGIVENESS DOES NOT MEAN ACCEPTING ABUSE.
Christian forgiveness does not require anyone to remain in a violent, abusive or dangerous relationship.

Where abuse exists, seek protection, professional assistance and appropriate legal support.

Safety must not be sacrificed in the name of preserving appearances.

5. HEALING REQUIRES TIME AND SUPPORT.
Psalm 147:3 reminds us that God heals the brokenhearted.

Healing may involve prayer, counselling, supportive relationships, healthy boundaries and time to process grief.

Do not pressure yourself to recover immediately.

6. YOUR FUTURE IS NOT CONTROLLED BY YOUR PAST RELATIONSHIP.
A failed relationship may change your circumstances, but it does not eliminate every possibility of a meaningful future.

There is still room for personal growth, meaningful relationships, service, purpose and happiness.
devotionals.reflection:
Have you allowed someone's rejection to make you question your worth?

Are you carrying bitterness, grief or disappointment that needs attention?

Are you remaining in an unsafe relationship because you fear what people will say?

Remember, you can experience heartbreak and still have a meaningful life.
devotionals.lesson: Never allow the failure of a relationship to become the reason you abandon your own life. Seek healing, establish healthy boundaries and receive appropriate support.
devotionals.prayer: Father, heal every wounded heart and comfort everyone experiencing relationship pain. Give strength to those facing separation, betrayal, divorce or bereavement. Deliver them from destructive thoughts and hopelessness. Grant wisdom to make healthy decisions and surround them with people who can support their healing, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Identify one unresolved emotional wound that needs attention. Take a positive step towards healing by speaking with a trusted counsellor, mature spiritual leader or qualified professional.

devotionals.title: You Are Not Alone in the Battle: The Power of Supportive Community
devotionals.keyVerse: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Galatians 6:2; Hebrews 10:24–25; Romans 12:10–15; 1 Thessalonians 5:11.

Human beings were not designed to live in complete isolation.

We need relationships, encouragement, companionship and practical support.

One of the dangers associated with suicidal thinking is isolation. When people withdraw from others, they may lose access to the encouragement and assistance that could help them through difficult seasons.

This is why families, churches, schools, workplaces and communities must take collective responsibility for supporting people who are emotionally distressed.

Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 teaches that two are better than one because when one falls, another can help lift that person.

This principle is especially important in suicide prevention.

1. COMMUNITY PROVIDES EMOTIONAL SUPPORT.
A supportive community gives people opportunities to express their fears, disappointments and struggles without being ridiculed.

Sometimes, knowing that somebody cares can make it easier to seek further help.

2. ISOLATION CAN MAKE EMOTIONAL DISTRESS WORSE.
When someone stops communicating, avoids friends and withdraws from meaningful activities, the people around them should pay attention.

Do not assume that silence means everything is fine.

Reach out and create opportunities for meaningful conversations.

3. FAMILIES MUST BECOME SAFE PLACES.
Parents should listen to their children without immediately shouting, condemning or comparing them with others.

Spouses should learn to discuss emotional struggles without humiliation.

Family members should understand that mental health difficulties require compassion, not ridicule.

4. CHURCHES MUST DEVELOP RESPONSIBLE SUPPORT SYSTEMS.
Churches should train pastors, chaplains and ministry leaders to recognise suicide warning signs and respond appropriately.

They should establish referral relationships with qualified mental health professionals.

Confidentiality must be handled responsibly, especially when someone's safety is at risk.

No pastor should attempt to manage an immediate suicide emergency alone.

5. SCHOOLS AND WORKPLACES MUST PROMOTE MENTAL WELLBEING.
Bullying, academic pressure, workplace harassment, discrimination and excessive expectations can contribute to emotional distress.

Institutions should develop clear reporting channels, supportive policies and access to appropriate counselling services.

6. SUPPORT MUST BE PRACTICAL, NOT JUST VERBAL.
Telling someone that you care is important, but practical support is equally necessary.

It may involve accompanying someone to a hospital, helping them access counselling, assisting with transportation, checking on them regularly or connecting them with reliable support services.

7. EVERYONE CAN CONTRIBUTE TO SAVING LIVES.
You do not need to be a psychiatrist to show compassion.

However, you must understand your limits and involve qualified professionals when necessary.

If someone is in immediate danger, remain with them, help keep them safe and obtain emergency medical assistance.
devotionals.reflection:
Are you part of a community where people feel safe discussing their emotional struggles?

Do you notice when people around you withdraw or become unusually discouraged?

Are you willing to support someone beyond offering religious advice?

A compassionate community can become a powerful protective environment for people experiencing emotional crises.
devotionals.lesson: Build relationships that provide emotional safety, encouragement and practical support. Never allow someone struggling with suicidal thoughts to face the crisis alone.
devotionals.prayer: Father, make our families, churches, schools and communities places of love, acceptance and genuine support. Deliver people from destructive isolation and connect those who are struggling with compassionate helpers and qualified professionals. Give us wisdom to recognise distress and courage to intervene responsibly. Let our lives become instruments of hope and preservation, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Identify one person who may be isolated or emotionally distressed. Reach out, listen and offer practical support. Also identify one trusted person you can approach when you need help.

devotionals.title: The Pain You Cannot Explain: Dealing with Emotional Trauma
devotionals.keyVerse: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Isaiah 61:1–3; Psalm 147:3; Genesis 50:20; 2 Corinthians 1:3–4.

Not every wound is visible. Some wounds are carried in the heart, buried in the memory and expressed through behaviour, relationships and emotional reactions.

Emotional trauma can result from experiences such as childhood abuse, sexual violence, domestic violence, bullying, betrayal, accidents, sudden loss, war, abandonment and other deeply distressing events.

Some people appear normal outwardly but are struggling internally with painful memories they cannot easily explain.

They may experience nightmares, fear, anxiety, emotional numbness, anger, shame, difficulty trusting others and persistent feelings of insecurity.

For some individuals, unresolved trauma can contribute to depression, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts.

We must understand that PEOPLE SHOULD NOT BE CONDEMNED FOR THE WOUNDS THEY ARE STRUGGLING TO HEAL.

1. TRAUMA IS REAL, EVEN WHEN NOBODY SEES IT.
A person may have experienced something deeply painful years ago and still struggle with its effects today.

Do not tell someone to forget an experience simply because it happened a long time ago.

Healing is not always immediate.

2. WHAT HAPPENED TO YOU DOES NOT DETERMINE YOUR WORTH.
People who have experienced sexual abuse, domestic violence, rejection or childhood neglect sometimes carry shame that does not belong to them.

The responsibility for abuse belongs to the perpetrator, not the victim.

Your painful experience does not make you dirty, useless or unworthy of love.

3. SUPPRESSED PAIN MAY REQUIRE PROFESSIONAL ATTENTION.
Some people try to bury traumatic experiences without addressing their emotional consequences.

Others turn to alcohol, drugs, isolation or destructive behaviour to escape painful memories.

Professional counselling and trauma-informed psychological treatment can help individuals process difficult experiences safely.

4. FORGIVENESS DOES NOT MEAN DENYING THE PAIN.
Christian forgiveness does not mean pretending that abuse never happened or allowing an offender to continue harming you.

You can pursue healing while maintaining necessary boundaries and seeking justice.

5. GOD IS PRESENT IN YOUR HEALING JOURNEY.
Psalm 34:18 reminds us that God is near to the brokenhearted.

God's compassion does not disappear because someone has experienced trauma.

He can provide strength through His Word, supportive relationships, pastoral care and professional treatment.

6. DO NOT ALLOW TRAUMA TO DESTROY YOUR FUTURE.
You may not be responsible for everything that happened to you, but you deserve support in deciding how to move forward.

If traumatic memories are accompanied by suicidal thoughts, seek urgent professional support. Do not face the crisis alone.
devotionals.reflection:
Are you carrying an emotional wound that you have never discussed with anybody?

Have you been blaming yourself for something another person did to you?

Have you allowed painful memories to convince you that your future cannot be better?

Your wounds deserve attention, not condemnation.
devotionals.lesson: Do not shame people for their traumatic experiences. Encourage healing, provide emotional safety and support access to appropriate professional care.
devotionals.prayer: Father, heal every wounded heart and restore those carrying painful memories. Deliver people from shame, fear, bitterness and emotional bondage. Give them access to compassionate support and appropriate professional treatment. Let their painful experiences no longer control their identity or destroy their hope, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: If you are carrying unresolved emotional pain, identify a qualified counsellor or mental health professional you can approach. If someone shares a traumatic experience with you, listen without blaming, questioning their worth or forcing them to disclose more than they are comfortable sharing.

devotionals.title: The Weight of Expectations: When Pressure Becomes Too Much
devotionals.keyVerse: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Psalm 55:22; Philippians 4:6–7; Isaiah 40:29; 1 Peter 5:7.

Many people are silently struggling under the weight of expectations.

Parents expect children to excel academically. Families expect their members to become financially successful. Churches expect their leaders to remain strong. Employers demand productivity. Society celebrates achievement and sometimes treats people who struggle as failures.

Consequently, some people live under constant pressure to meet expectations they cannot realistically sustain.

Students fear disappointing their parents. Young adults fear being unsuccessful. Married couples struggle to meet financial and social expectations. Ministers fear that admitting emotional difficulties will damage their reputation.

When pressure becomes overwhelming, some people begin to experience anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts.

We must understand that NO HUMAN BEING WAS CREATED TO LIVE UNDER UNLIMITED PRESSURE.

1. YOU ARE NOT REQUIRED TO PLEASE EVERYBODY.
Trying to satisfy everybody can become emotionally exhausting.

People will always have different expectations, opinions and demands.

Learn to recognise what is reasonable, what is necessary and what you must respectfully decline.

2. YOUR WORTH IS NOT MEASURED BY YOUR PERFORMANCE.
A student who fails an examination is still valuable.

An employee who loses a job is still valuable.

A minister who experiences a difficult season is still valuable.

Your achievements may change, but your human dignity remains.

3. LEARN TO RECOGNISE YOUR LIMITS.
Even Jesus withdrew from crowds to rest and pray (Luke 5:16).

Rest is not laziness. Taking breaks is not irresponsibility. Asking for assistance is not weakness.

Recognising your limits is part of responsible living.

4. DO NOT COMPARE YOUR JOURNEY WITH OTHER PEOPLE'S ACHIEVEMENTS.
Social media often presents carefully selected pictures of people's successes while hiding their struggles.

Comparing your private difficulties with another person's public achievements can increase feelings of inadequacy.

Your journey is different. Concentrate on responsible growth rather than unhealthy competition.

5. BREAK OVERWHELMING RESPONSIBILITIES INTO MANAGEABLE STEPS.
When everything appears urgent, identify the most important task and address it one step at a time.

Seek assistance where necessary. Delegate responsibilities. Develop realistic plans and allow yourself adequate rest.

6. NEVER ALLOW PRESSURE TO DRIVE YOU TOWARDS SELF-DESTRUCTION.
If pressure is producing persistent hopelessness or suicidal thoughts, speak with someone trustworthy and seek professional help.

If you feel you may act on those thoughts, do not remain alone. Seek emergency medical assistance.
devotionals.reflection:
What expectations are currently placing the greatest pressure on your life?

Are you trying to prove your worth through achievements?

Have you forgotten that you are human and that you also need rest, encouragement and support?

You do not have to destroy yourself to satisfy other people's expectations.
devotionals.lesson: Live responsibly without making the expectations of others more important than your health, safety and wellbeing.
devotionals.prayer: Father, deliver me from destructive pressure, unhealthy competition and the fear of disappointing people. Teach me to recognise my limitations, organise my responsibilities and receive help when necessary. Give me peace in difficult seasons and strength to continue without losing my emotional wellbeing, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Identify three pressures currently affecting your life. Determine which ones you can address immediately, which require assistance and which expectations you need to reconsider.

devotionals.title: Young, but Not Without Purpose: Protecting Our Youths from Suicidal Thoughts
devotionals.keyVerse: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Ecclesiastes 12:1; Jeremiah 1:7–8; Psalm 71:17–18; Isaiah 40:30–31.

Young people are among the most important investments of every society, yet many are silently battling emotional and psychological challenges.

Academic pressure, unemployment, cyberbullying, relationship disappointments, family instability, substance abuse, sexual exploitation, financial hardship and social comparison can create enormous pressure for young people.

Some teenagers feel that their parents do not understand them. Some university students are overwhelmed by academic expectations. Some graduates feel ashamed because they cannot secure employment. Others believe their lives have failed because they cannot meet the standards presented on social media.

When these pressures become overwhelming, some young people may develop suicidal thoughts.

We must stop assuming that young people are automatically happy simply because they are young.

1. YOUTH DOES NOT ELIMINATE EMOTIONAL PAIN.
A teenager can experience depression. A university student can experience severe anxiety. A young graduate can experience hopelessness.

Age does not make anyone immune to mental health difficulties.

2. ACADEMIC FAILURE IS NOT LIFE FAILURE.
Some young people believe that failing an examination means disappointing their entire family.

Others fear being compared with siblings or classmates.

Parents and teachers must communicate that academic performance is important but does not determine the total value of a person's life.

There are different pathways to learning, growth and meaningful achievement.

3. CYBERBULLYING AND SOCIAL MEDIA PRESSURE MUST BE TAKEN SERIOUSLY.
Online humiliation, threats, sexual exploitation, harmful comparisons and public embarrassment can deeply affect young people's emotional wellbeing.

Parents and schools should create safe reporting systems and respond appropriately to cyberbullying.

4. PARENTS MUST LEARN TO LISTEN.
Some parents communicate with their children only through instructions, correction and punishment.

Young people also need opportunities to discuss their fears, friendships, disappointments and emotional struggles.

Do not make your home a place where children are afraid to tell the truth.

5. THE CHURCH MUST PROVIDE MORE THAN RELIGIOUS ACTIVITIES.
Youth ministries should promote emotional wellbeing, healthy relationships, responsible decision-making and access to professional support.

Pastors and youth leaders must know when to refer a struggling young person to qualified mental health professionals.

6. YOUNG PEOPLE MUST UNDERSTAND THAT THEIR FUTURE IS NOT FINISHED.
Unemployment, examination failure, relationship disappointment and financial limitations do not mean that life has no meaning.

There are opportunities to learn, grow, recover and begin again.

If a young person expresses suicidal thoughts, take them seriously, involve responsible adults and qualified professionals, and ensure immediate safety where necessary.
devotionals.reflection:
Parents: Do your children feel safe discussing their emotional struggles with you?

Teachers: Do your students see you as someone they can approach when life becomes difficult?

Young people: Have you allowed temporary challenges to make you question your future?

Your youth is not a wasted season. Your life has value beyond your present achievements.
devotionals.lesson: Protect young people by creating environments where they can communicate freely, receive appropriate guidance and access mental health support without stigma.
devotionals.prayer: Father, preserve our children and young people. Protect them from destructive influences, emotional oppression, exploitation and hopelessness. Give parents wisdom, teachers compassion and youth leaders understanding. Raise a generation that values life, seeks help when necessary and fulfils its God-given potential, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Parents and guardians should have a meaningful conversation with a young person today. Ask about their emotional wellbeing, not just their academic performance or achievements. Young people should identify a trusted adult they can approach whenever they experience overwhelming emotional difficulties.

devotionals.title: Love That Saves: The Power of Genuine Love and Compassion
devotionals.keyVerse: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: John 13:34–35; 1 Corinthians 13:4–7; Romans 12:10; Galatians 6:2.

Love is more than romantic feelings, gifts, celebrations and public expressions of affection.

Genuine love involves understanding, patience, sacrifice, compassion and responsibility towards others.

On a day when many people celebrate romantic relationships, we must remember those who are struggling with loneliness, rejection, broken marriages, bereavement and emotional pain.

For some people, Valentine's Day can intensify feelings of abandonment and inadequacy.

Some compare their relationships with what they see around them. Others remember failed relationships or painful experiences. Some feel forgotten because nobody has expressed affection towards them.

We must communicate an important truth: YOUR VALUE IS NOT DETERMINED BY WHETHER SOMEBODY IS ROMANTICALLY ATTRACTED TO YOU.

1. LOVE MUST GO BEYOND WORDS.
It is easy to say that we love people, but genuine love is demonstrated through our actions.

A person experiencing depression needs more than inspirational quotations. They may need someone to listen, accompany them to an appointment or help them access treatment.

2. LOVE DOES NOT HUMILIATE PEOPLE.
Do not use people's weaknesses, failures, financial conditions or emotional struggles as opportunities to ridicule them.

A compassionate person corrects without destroying dignity.

3. LOVE REQUIRES US TO NOTICE PEOPLE.
Some people are surrounded by others but remain emotionally neglected.

Learn to recognise when someone is withdrawn, discouraged or struggling.

A simple conversation can create an opportunity for someone to receive help.

4. LOVE MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH UNHEALTHY DEPENDENCE.
Your happiness and identity should not be entirely dependent on another human being.

Healthy relationships encourage respect, safety, personal growth and mutual responsibility.

No one should remain in an abusive relationship because they believe suffering is the proof of love.

5. GOD'S LOVE IS NOT LIMITED TO ROMANTIC RELATIONSHIPS.
God's love is constant and unconditional.

Romans 8:38–39 reminds us that neither death, life nor any other created thing can separate believers from the love of God.

Human rejection cannot cancel God's love.

6. BECOME AN INSTRUMENT OF LIFE-PRESERVING LOVE.
Sometimes the most meaningful expression of love is recognising that somebody needs help and ensuring they receive it.

If someone discloses suicidal thoughts, listen, take the disclosure seriously and connect them with appropriate professional support.
devotionals.reflection:
Who around you needs genuine love rather than criticism?

Have you confused romantic acceptance with personal worth?

Are you demonstrating love through practical care?

The world needs more people who can listen without condemning, encourage without manipulating and support without humiliating.
devotionals.lesson: Demonstrate love through compassion, patience, understanding and practical support. Never use another person's emotional struggles as an opportunity to shame them.
devotionals.prayer: Father, fill my heart with genuine love and compassion. Deliver me from selfishness, bitterness and the tendency to condemn people who are struggling. Help me recognise the needs of others and become an instrument of encouragement, healing and hope. Let my life reflect the love of Christ, in Jesus' name. Amen.
devotionals.actionPoint: Show genuine love to three people today. One may be a family member, another a friend and another someone who is lonely or emotionally distressed. Let your love be expressed through meaningful action.

devotionals.title: When Substance Abuse Takes Control: Breaking the Cycle of Destruction
devotionals.keyVerse: All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.
devotionals.introduction:
Monthly Theme: Dealing with Suicide.

Supporting Scriptures: Proverbs 20:1; Ephesians 5:18; Galatians 5:22–23; 1 Peter 5:8.

Substance abuse is a serious public health and social challenge that affects individuals, families and communities.

Alcohol, cannabis, opioids, prescription medicines used improperly and other psychoactive substances can affect the brain, judgement, behaviour and emotional stability.

Some people begin using substances out of curiosity. Others use them because of peer pressure, depression, anxiety, trauma, loneliness or the desire to escape painful realities.

Unfortunately, substance misuse can worsen the very problems people are trying to escape.

It can contribute to family breakdown, financial difficulties, violence, accidents, mental health complications and suicidal behaviour.

We must understand that SUBSTANCE ABUSE IS NOT JUST A PERSONAL HABIT; IT CAN BECOME A SERIOUS HEALTH CONDITION REQUIRING PROFESSIONAL TREATMENT.
